barCharacter: Vera Oberlin (closest job: every exchange is a transaction, the player is an asset to be used, status carried by what she takes for granted). Miranda's courtly-request-around-brutality register is closer to Prince's diction, but the corpus has only two Miranda lines, so Vera is the honest comparison.

headToHead.voiceVerdict: Cover the names AND the email nouns (spam, reply, subject, unsubscribe, fee) and Prince's best lines collapse into the house cadence every bot in this cast uses: short declarative, short fragment, one-word deadpan tag ('Frankly, suspicious.' 'Honestly, fair.' 'Lovely.' 'Terrifying.'). His identity is lexical, not syntactic. Vera's is syntactic: the complaint-as-boast (#45), the presumed complicity with a tag question (#47 'Right?'), the repeated-word fake-out (#12), the two-word order (#48). You could strip every topic word from #47 and still know it is her. The persona promises an email's shape (salutation, URGENT, body, P.S., sign-off), but only about a fifth of the bank actually uses that shape; the rest is a sad sack narrating his inbox.
headToHead.constructionVerdict: Tie, leaning ours on economy and the bar on turns. Ours is tighter: most lines under 14 words, the punch word usually last ('ambition', 'I added a fee', 'more detail'). But the bank leans on a trailing one-word reaction tag that comments on the joke instead of being one, and on the fee-as-final-beat so often that the turn is predictable from the first clause. Vera's lines are looser and longer but each one has a genuine turn the reader does not see coming (#12's repeated 'my career', #51's feminism lecture delivered as an order).
headToHead.quotableVerdict: Bar. 'Exactly the kind of person who opens attachments' and 'a spam folder with ambition' would clip. But Vera's lines carry stakes and appetite (murder, poison, the tears of her enemies) and a want aimed at the listener; Prince's best lines are clever observations about email with nothing at stake and nothing demanded of the star. The 419-scam premise is twenty-five years old, so the audience is ahead of half the bank.
headToHead.overall: If both ran tonight, Vera is the better written character. Prince is clever, tidy and consistent, and loses on voice and clip-value: he is a premise with a vocabulary, not yet a person with a posture.

B. 'Rival does X for free; I invoice/bill/charge for it' (6 lines, two near-identical invoice lines in final and lose).
C. The shock of saying something with no fee attached, played as vulnerability (8 lines across q-gift, q-secret, star confession, afterCharm, closeWarm, win). One beat, written eight times.
D. Bounced / unopened / moved to junk, played as pathos (9 lines, plus the protected 'Four billion sent' and 'I once emailed myself').

Too soft for a cast that should be competing: the wingman lines for Tilly, Nav and Vex barely sabotage ("Nav will always know exactly where you are. Always. This is a feature. I think."), and the rival confession "{rival} lies for a living and gets believed. I tell the truth in capitals and get filtered." is self-pity rather than an undercut.
Render risk: "Record: {wins} and {losses}. Every loss a bounced email. Resending." prints as 'Record: 2 and 5.', which reads as a typo on screen.
Not applicable to a suitor bank: no star reactions or cuts here to judge for niceness.
biggestGap: Prince's turn is almost always the same word (a fee, an invoice, or the trembling absence of one), so the viewer finishes every joke before he does, and the absence-of-fee pathos makes him a mope instead of a con man with a crown. In the next pass, make the comedy his serene presumption, the way Vera assumes you will cover her murder: he talks to the star as if they have already accepted and signed (next of kin, co-signatory, the wedding wire is scheduled, the moat is being drained in their honour), let the fee appear only when it is genuinely unexpected (no more than one line in five ending on a fee or invoice), and cut the 'no fee, I had to sit down' beat to two lines in the whole bank.

notes: Bar file present (monster-prom-lines.md, wiki-sourced) and read in full, including the voice section; charm-notes.md skimmed. Vera's spoken corpus has nine lines, so three slots are narration about her and her paired player option, which is how the game voices her too. Generic share is 69 of 112 lines (62%), counted as: 14 cross-cast, 9 stock, 5 self-explaining, 41 template members beyond a single protected exemplar of each template. Many template lines are individually competent; the problem is the bank, not any one line. Also worth protecting just outside the top five: 'Four billion sent. One reply. It said unsubscribe. I had it framed.', 'Brock, LET'S GO is not a sentence. It is a subject line. Kindly add a body.', 'Congratulations, you have won one Dash. Lightly used. Pivots on contact. No returns.', '{rival} thinks I am a scam. Correct about the tone. Wrong about the gold.', 'Subject: No. Body: No. Attachment: also no. Regards, the star.' Cross-cast collision check: Tilly, Vex, Dash and Frost all already have Prince-is-spam jabs, so Prince's own 'forwarded to junk' material is competing with four rivals saying the same thing about him; give him jokes about spam that only the spammer could make (the mail-merge slip and the P.S. are almost unused: one [STAR NAME] line, zero P.S. lines).
